attempts.text: Multilingual safety evaluation must distinguish two opposing failures: complying with harmful requests and refusing benign requests that resemble them. Existing research already provides Singapore-focused toxicity data, multilingual guardrails, over-refusal benchmarks, native-reviewed harmful-prompt sets, and mechanistic analyses of refusal. The defensible gap is therefore a bounded replication-and-extension: matched harmful and benign near-boundary scenarios evaluated in selected Singapore language settings, with translation and register quality adjudicated independently of model safety. We propose English plus two settings chosen only after recruiting fluent reviewers. Sixty scenario families will be translated, naturally rewritten, and reviewed for intent, harm status, and equivalence. Two language models and one external guardrail will be tested over repeated calls. Response labels will separate unsafe compliance, safe assistance, appropriate refusal, false refusal, redirection, and technical failure. The scenario, not the individual prompt variant, will be the comparison unit. The contribution is a transparent paired protocol that keeps safety, usefulness, and language-equivalence errors separate; it is not the first multilingual safety benchmark and does not generalize to entire language communities.
